verses.text: Do you not know, brothers (for I am speaking to those who know the law), that the law has authority over a man only as long as he lives?
For instance, a married woman is bound by law to her husband as long as he lives. But if her husband dies, she is released from the law of marriage.

So then, if she is joined to another man while her husband is still alive, she is called an adulteress; but if her husband dies, she is free from that law and is not an adulteress, even if she marries another man.
Therefore, my brothers, you also died to the law through the body of Christ, that you might belong to another, to Him who was raised from the dead, in order that we might bear fruit to God.
For when we lived according to the flesh, the sinful passions aroused by the law were at work in our bodies, bearing fruit for death.
But now, having died to what bound us, we have been released from the law, so that we serve in the new way of the Spirit, and not in the old way of the written code.

What then shall we say? Is the law sin? Certainly not! Indeed, I would not have been mindful of sin if not for the law. For I would not have been aware of coveting if the law had not said, "Do not covet."
But sin, seizing its opportunity through the commandment, produced in me every kind of covetous desire. For apart from the law, sin is dead.
Once I was alive apart from the law; but when the commandment came, sin sprang to life and I died.
So I discovered that the very commandment that was meant to bring life actually brought death.
For sin, seizing its opportunity through the commandment, deceived me and through the commandment put me to death.
So then, the law is holy, and the commandment is holy, righteous, and good.

Did that which is good, then, become death to me? Certainly not! But in order that sin might be exposed as sin, it produced death in me through what was good, so that through the commandment sin might become utterly sinful.
We know that the law is spiritual; but I am unspiritual, sold as a slave to sin.
I do not understand what I do. For what I want to do, I do not do. But what I hate, I do.
And if I do what I do not want to do, I admit that the law is good.
In that case, it is no longer I who do it, but it is sin living in me that does it.
I know that nothing good lives in me, that is, in my flesh; for I have the desire to do what is good, but I cannot carry it out.
For I do not do the good I want to do. Instead, I keep on doing the evil I do not want to do.
And if I do what I do not want, it is no longer I who do it, but it is sin living in me that does it.
So this is the principle I have discovered: When I want to do good, evil is right there with me.
For in my inner being I delight in God's law.
But I see another law at work in my body, warring against the law of my mind and holding me captive to the law of sin that dwells within me.
What a wretched man I am! Who will rescue me from this body of death?
Thanks be to God, through Jesus Christ our Lord! So then, with my mind I serve the law of God, but with my flesh I serve the law of sin.

context.author: Paul the apostle, writing through a secretary named Tertius (1:1; 16:22)
context.genre: Letter (epistle), written as a carefully argued case for the gospel
context.audience: The Christians in Rome, a mixed community of Jews and Gentiles
context.mapLabel: ROME, THE LAW AND THE DIVIDED SELF
context.setting: Paul explains how believers are released from the law, using an example from marriage. Then he asks if the law is sin, and answers no: it shows sin up. The last half describes a person who wants to do what is right but can’t, and cries out for rescue.
context.custom: In Roman and Jewish law, a married woman was bound to her husband until his death. Paul uses it as a picture: believers died with Christ, so the old tie to the law is ended and they belong to someone new.
context.timelineImmediate: Chapter 8 begins with the answer to the cry in 7:24: “There is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.”
context.timelineBible: The command “You shall not covet” (v.7) is the tenth commandment (Exodus 20:17). Paul’s picture of sin deceiving him (v.11) recalls the serpent in Genesis 3:13.
context.sparkNotes: Paul says the law is holy, but it shows sin up and cannot give life. He describes a conflict where he wants the good but does the evil he hates. He cries out, “Who will rescue me?” and answers, “Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord!”

translation.meaning: Worn out and miserable, the cry of a person at the end of his strength.
In Paul it often means human nature apart from God, not simply the body.

otBackground.note: “You shall not covet,” the commandment that exposed Paul’s sin.
The serpent deceived Eve, and Paul says sin deceived him.
The word is near, a text Paul will use in chapter 10.

overview.summary: Believers are free from the law as a way to be made right. The law is good but exposes sin, and the struggle between wanting good and doing evil is answered by Christ.
overview.settingLine: Paul writes from Corinth to the Christians in Rome.

history.t: Readers have long disagreed whether Paul describes his life before Christ, his life as a believer, or Israel under the law.
Paul insists the law is holy, righteous, and good (v.12). The problem is sin.

customs.t: The tenth commandment deals with desire, not action, which is where Paul says he saw his sin.
A woman was bound to her husband while he lived, and free to remarry after his death.

archaeology.t: Stone tablets with the commandments are described in Exodus 20 and later copied on synagogue walls.
Small leather boxes with Scripture, found at Qumran, show the effort to keep the law before the eyes.

overview.discussion: Paul says, “I do not do the good I want to do.” How do I respond to my own failures, and where do I look for help?
overview.book: The letter to the Romans · 16 chapters. Paul’s fullest explanation of the gospel, written to a church he had not yet visited.
overview.author: Paul

historicalImage.caption: Paul in Prison, by Rembrandt (1627). It is an imagined scene: Romans was not written from prison, but the painting suits Paul's cry in Romans 7:24.

currentImage.caption: The synagogue at Ostia, the port of Rome. What stands today was rebuilt in the 4th century, though the first building may go back to the 1st. It shows the kind of Jewish community living near the Christians Paul wrote to.
